solution.concept_anchor: Attlee Declaration February 1947 deadline
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is a strong distractor because students familiar with Mountbatten associate him with the June 1948 deadline change, confusing the original Attlee Declaration deadline with Mountbatten's revision.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: the Attlee Declaration of February 1947 announced Britain's intention to withdraw from India, not a specific constitutional framework.
Eliminate option b: the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) is distinct from the Attlee Declaration — they are separate interventions.
Eliminate option d: August 1947 was the accelerated deadline Mountbatten chose — the Attlee Declaration originally set June 1948.
Confirm option c: Attlee's February 1947 declaration specified June 1948 as the deadline for British withdrawal, which Mountbatten subsequently advanced.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students frequently conflate the Attlee Declaration (February 1947) with the Mountbatten Plan (June 1947) or with the actual transfer date (August 15, 1947). The trap exploits the existence of three distinct deadlines — June 1948 (Attlee), August 1947 (Mountbatten's revision), and August 15, 1947 (actual transfer) — causing students to assign August 1947 to the Attlee Declaration itself.
solution.final_explanation:
The Attlee Declaration of February 20, 1947 was the British government's formal announcement that it intended to transfer power to Indian hands no later than June 1948. This set the political clock ticking but provided no structural plan for how power would be transferred.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The Attlee Declaration did not unveil a constitutional framework — it only committed to a withdrawal timeline.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) preceded the Attlee Declaration and proposed a federated united India with groupings — a distinct exercise.
• Option (c): Correct. June 1948 was the original deadline stated in the Attlee Declaration. Mountbatten subsequently accelerated this to August 1947 upon assessing the deteriorating communal situation.
• Option (d): Incorrect. August 1947 was Mountbatten's revised deadline, not Attlee's original commitment.

Value Addition:
• Lord Wavell was replaced by Mountbatten precisely because Wavell's 'Breakdown Plan' lacked political acceptability.
• Attlee's Labour government was ideologically committed to Indian independence but faced strategic pressures over Commonwealth membership.
• The acceleration from June 1948 to August 1947 gave barely 73 days for the Radcliffe Commission to demarcate boundaries.

solution.concept_anchor: Sylhet referendum unique district-level status

statement_analysis.statement: The Sylhet referendum was the only district-level referendum held under the Mountbatten Plan, making it unique among all the plebiscitary exercises conducted in 1947.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike NWFP, which was a province-level referendum, Sylhet was a single district within Assam that voted separately on whether to join East Bengal (Pakistan) — the only instance of a district-level referendum in the entire partition process.

statement_analysis.statement: The Congress party boycotted the NWFP referendum, and as a consequence, the referendum resulted in a vote in favour of joining Pakistan.
statement_analysis.reason: Congress, along with Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan's Khudai Khidmatgar movement, boycotted the NWFP referendum on the grounds that 'Pakhtunistan' was not an option on the ballot. The referendum still resulted in a majority voting for Pakistan, though voter turnout was significantly reduced.

statement_analysis.statement: Baluchistan's decision to join Pakistan was made through a province-wide referendum similar to the one held in NWFP.
statement_analysis.reason: Baluchistan did not hold a popular referendum. The decision was made by the Shahi Jirga (a traditional non-elected assembly) and the Quetta Municipality — a process criticised for lacking democratic representation.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) is a strong distractor because students who know statements 1 and 2 are correct assume statement 3 must follow the same referendum pattern, not realising Baluchistan used the Shahi Jirga mechanism.
elimination_logic: Verify statement 1: Sylhet was indeed the only district-level vote — NWFP, Sind, Bengal, and Punjab operated at provincial or assembly level. Statement 1 is correct.
Verify statement 2: Congress did boycott the NWFP referendum, and Pakistan won the vote — both parts of statement 2 are accurate.
Verify statement 3: Baluchistan never had a popular referendum — the Shahi Jirga, a traditional non-elected body, decided; this disqualifies statement 3.
Only statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in statement 3 exploits the assumption that all provinces followed the same referendum mechanism. Students who know NWFP held a referendum incorrectly extend this to Baluchistan. The Shahi Jirga is a factual detail that directly contradicts the 'referendum' framing — only students with precise knowledge of Baluchistan's unique procedure will eliminate statement 3.
solution.final_explanation:
The Mountbatten Plan prescribed different mechanisms for different provinces to decide their future, reflecting ground realities rather than uniform democratic principles.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Sylhet, a district of Assam with a Muslim-majority population, held the only district-level referendum. It voted to merge with East Bengal (Pakistan), altering Assam's composition significantly.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Congress and the Khudai Khidmatgar boycotted the NWFP referendum, arguing that an independent Pakhtunistan option was absent. The vote proceeded and returned a majority for Pakistan, though the turnout was low due to the boycott.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Baluchistan's accession was decided by the Shahi Jirga, a traditional tribal assembly of non-elected members, alongside the Quetta Municipality — not by a popular referendum. This remains one of the most criticised aspects of the partition process for its democratic deficit.

Value Addition:
• Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, known as 'Frontier Gandhi,' never reconciled with Pakistan's formation and was repeatedly imprisoned by Pakistani authorities.
• The Sylhet referendum result meant Assam lost a significant Muslim-majority district, reshaping the demographic character of East Pakistan.
• The Shahi Jirga precedent in Baluchistan later fuelled Baloch nationalist sentiment about the involuntary nature of their accession.

solution.concept_anchor: Baluchistan Shahi Jirga non-elected body partition decision

statement_analysis.statement: The Bengal Legislative Assembly met as a single unified body to vote on whether Bengal as a whole should join Pakistan or remain with India.
statement_analysis.reason: The Bengal Legislative Assembly met in two separate parts — members representing predominantly Hindu-majority western districts met separately from members representing Muslim-majority eastern districts. Each part voted independently, leading to the partition of Bengal.

statement_analysis.statement: The Sind Legislative Assembly voted in favour of joining Pakistan without a separate referendum being held among the Sind population.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike NWFP and Sylhet, Sind did not hold a popular referendum. The Sind Legislative Assembly itself voted on the question of joining Pakistan, and the assembly voted in favour — no separate plebiscite was conducted.

statement_analysis.statement: The Shahi Jirga in Baluchistan, which voted on accession to Pakistan, was a fully elected representative body constituted specifically for this purpose under the Mountbatten Plan.
statement_analysis.reason: The Shahi Jirga was a traditional, non-elected tribal assembly — not a constituted elected body. Its use was widely criticised as undemocratic. The Quetta Municipality also participated, but neither constituted a universal franchise exercise.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify statement 1 as incorrect may assume statement 3 is correct, not knowing that the Shahi Jirga was non-elected.
elimination_logic: Evaluate statement 1: the Bengal assembly did NOT meet as a unified body — it met in two separate parts by regional composition. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate statement 2: Sind did vote through its Legislative Assembly without a referendum — this is factually accurate. Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate statement 3: the Shahi Jirga was a traditional tribal assembly, not an elected body created under the Mountbatten Plan. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 conflates 'traditional assembly' with 'elected representative body.' Students who know a body called 'Shahi Jirga' made the decision for Baluchistan may assume it was constituted properly for this purpose, not recognising its non-elected, customary character. Statement 1 traps students who know Bengal was partitioned but forget the procedural detail that the assembly met in two separate parts rather than one combined sitting.
solution.final_explanation:
The Mountbatten Plan prescribed province-specific procedures rather than a uniform mechanism, creating procedural variation that is a frequent UPSC testing area.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Bengal Legislative Assembly did not meet as a single unified body. Members from the western (Hindu-majority) districts met separately from members of the eastern (Muslim-majority) districts. The western members voted for partition and remaining with India; the eastern members voted for joining Pakistan — thus confirming the partition of Bengal.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Sind used its Legislative Assembly as the decision-making body. The assembly voted to join Pakistan, and no separate public referendum was conducted in Sind.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Shahi Jirga was a traditional, non-elected tribal institution — not a democratically constituted assembly created for this purpose. Its use drew criticism as it did not reflect universal franchise.

Value Addition:
• The Punjab Legislative Assembly similarly met in two parts, with western Punjab voting for Pakistan and eastern Punjab voting to remain with India.
• The use of existing legislatures (rather than referendums) in Bengal, Punjab, and Sind was designed to speed up the process under Mountbatten's accelerated timeline.
• Balochistan's undemocratic accession process remains a grievance cited by Baloch nationalist movements to this day.

solution.concept_anchor: Radcliffe Commission composition and mandate

statement_analysis.statement: Sir Cyril Radcliffe was appointed as chairman of both the Punjab and Bengal boundary commissions.
statement_analysis.reason: Radcliffe chaired both boundary commissions simultaneously — one for Punjab and one for Bengal — and his lack of prior India knowledge was considered an advantage for impartiality.

statement_analysis.statement: The Radcliffe Award was announced on August 15, 1947 — Independence Day itself — so that both nations received the boundary details simultaneously.
statement_analysis.reason: The Radcliffe Award was deliberately withheld and announced on August 17, 1947 — two days after Independence Day — to prevent communal violence from intensifying before the transfer of power.

statement_analysis.statement: The boundary commissions' mandate included 'other factors' beyond contiguous majority areas, giving Radcliffe discretionary latitude in demarcation.
statement_analysis.reason: The terms of reference explicitly included 'other factors' alongside majority-area criteria, allowing Radcliffe considerable discretion — a source of lasting controversy, particularly regarding Gurdaspur district.

statement_analysis.statement: Each boundary commission had equal representation from both the Muslim League and the Congress, and decisions required a unanimous vote of all members.
statement_analysis.reason: While each commission did have equal representation from both sides (two members each from Congress and the Muslim League), unanimous decisions were not required. In practice, the four members consistently voted along communal lines (2-2 deadlock), leaving Radcliffe to make the final award unilaterally.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (only two) is a strong distractor because students who correctly reject statement 2 but are uncertain about statement 4's deadlock mechanism may count only statements 1 and 3 as correct, which is actually correct — but option b labels it 'only two,' which matches, making it a close call between b and c.
elimination_logic: Evaluate statement 1: Radcliffe chaired both Punjab and Bengal commissions — correct.
Evaluate statement 2: the award was announced August 17, not August 15 — incorrect; the secret was maintained past Independence Day.
Evaluate statement 3: 'other factors' were explicitly in the mandate — correct.
Evaluate statement 4: decisions did not require unanimity — the 2-2 deadlock meant Radcliffe decided alone; unanimous vote requirement is false.
Two statements (1 and 3) are correct — select option b... wait: options are (a) Only one, (b) Only two, (c) Only three, (d) All four. Only two correct → option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the very common misconception that the Radcliffe Award was revealed on Independence Day itself (August 15, 1947). Mountbatten deliberately withheld the award until August 17 to avoid mass violence disrupting the transfer-of-power ceremonies. Statement 4 traps students who know about equal representation but assume this translated into a requirement for consensus.
solution.final_explanation:
The Radcliffe Commission is one of the most consequential and contested administrative exercises in South Asian history. Its composition and procedure were carefully designed — though the outcomes remain debated.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had never visited India, was chosen precisely to ensure nominal impartiality. He chaired both the Punjab and Bengal commissions concurrently.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The award was kept secret and released on August 17, 1947 — two days after Independence Day. Mountbatten's reasoning was that releasing it before August 15 would inflame communal tensions during the transfer ceremonies.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The mandate included 'other factors' beyond simple majority demographics, giving Radcliffe latitude that shaped critical decisions — most notably the allocation of Gurdaspur, which gave India a land route to Kashmir.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The 2-2 voting deadlock (Congress nominees vs. Muslim League nominees) was anticipated, and the design effectively made Radcliffe the sole decision-maker from the outset.

Value Addition:
• Radcliffe destroyed all his personal papers related to the award after returning to Britain, fuelling decades of speculation.
• Gurdaspur's allocation to India is frequently cited as enabling India's accession of Kashmir — a geopolitically transformative consequence of the 'other factors' clause.
• Radcliffe received no additional payment for his work beyond his standard fee and returned it, reportedly out of distaste for the outcome.

solution.concept_anchor: Cabinet Mission vs Mountbatten Plan structural differences
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because students may correctly place A-2 (Cabinet Mission rejecting two-nation theory) but then incorrectly match B-1 (confusing the grouping scheme with Mountbatten's dominion formula), leading them to option b.
elimination_logic: Match A: The Cabinet Mission Plan explicitly rejected the two-nation theory and proposed a united India with groupings — matches description 2.
Match B: The Mountbatten Plan created two separate sovereign dominions with dominion status — matches description 1.
Match C: The Cabinet Mission's treatment of princely states involved an advisory committee on states within the federal structure — matches description 4.
Match D: The Mountbatten Plan declared the lapse of British paramountcy, leaving states free to accede — matches description 3.
Correct matching: A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3 → option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in conflating the two plans' approaches to princely states. Students who know paramountcy lapsed under the Mountbatten Plan may incorrectly assign it to the Cabinet Mission column. Similarly, the 'grouping scheme' and 'federal structure' sound like they could belong to either plan to a surface-level reader. Precise knowledge of which plan did what is essential.
solution.final_explanation:
The Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) and Mountbatten Plan (1947) represent fundamentally different approaches to Indian independence — one seeking unity, the other managing division.

Correct matches:
• A (Cabinet Mission) — 2: The Cabinet Mission explicitly rejected the two-nation theory and proposed a three-tier federal structure with provinces grouped into sections, keeping India united.
• B (Mountbatten Plan) — 1: The Mountbatten Plan operationalised partition by creating two separate dominions — India and Pakistan — both within the British Commonwealth, with dominion status rather than full immediate independence.
• C (Cabinet Mission — Princely States) — 4: The Cabinet Mission proposed an advisory committee to negotiate the relationship between princely states and the proposed union, integrating them into the federal scheme.
• D (Mountbatten Plan — Princely States) — 3: The Mountbatten Plan announced that British paramountcy would lapse on the date of independence, leaving each princely state technically free to choose between accession to India, Pakistan, or independence.

Value Addition:
• Congress rejected the Cabinet Mission's grouping scheme because Group B and Group C would have given Muslim League effective control over large territories.
• Paramountcy lapsing without automatic merger created the crises of Hyderabad, Junagadh, and Kashmir.
• Both plans accepted dominion status, but the Cabinet Mission envisaged a single dominion while Mountbatten created two.

solution.concept_anchor: Jinnah as Pakistan Governor-General two-dominion theory significance
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students correctly identify both A and R as factually true and assume causal connection, not recognising that Jinnah's motivation was political consolidation of power, not a philosophical statement about the two-nation theory.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Jinnah became Pakistan's first Governor-General while Mountbatten became India's first Governor-General; they were separate appointments.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Jinnah did want maximum executive authority over Pakistan in its critical early months, and becoming Governor-General (which held real executive power under dominion status) rather than Prime Minister served this goal.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. R explains why Jinnah chose the Governor-General role over Prime Minister, but A simply states the fact that separate Governors-General were appointed. R does not explain why separate appointments were made — that follows from the plan's two-dominion structure. The causal link is broken.

A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → option b... wait: re-reading — A states the fact of separate GGs; R explains Jinnah's personal motivation for taking the GG role. R explains Jinnah's individual decision, not the structural fact that there were separate GGs. → option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both A and R are independently true. The trap is that R (Jinnah's desire for executive authority) feels like it explains A (separate Governor-Generals). But A is a structural provision of the Mountbatten Plan — two dominions naturally required two Governors-General. R explains Jinnah's personal choice within that structure, not the structure itself. Students who verify both as true immediately pick option a without testing the causal link.
solution.final_explanation:
The appointment of separate Governors-General for India and Pakistan was a direct consequence of the two-dominion structure in the Mountbatten Plan. Under dominion status, the Governor-General exercised significant constitutional authority — not a merely ceremonial role.

Assertion (A): Factually correct. Mountbatten became India's first Governor-General, while Jinnah chose to become Pakistan's first Governor-General. This was structurally required by the two-dominion arrangement.

Reason (R): Factually correct. Jinnah rejected the initial suggestion that Mountbatten serve as a common Governor-General for both dominions, partly because he wanted direct personal control over Pakistan's formative governance. As Governor-General under dominion status, he held real executive authority, unlike the largely ceremonial Prime Minister position in Westminster systems.

Causal link: R does not explain A. A (the existence of separate Governors-General) flows from the plan's two-dominion structure, not from Jinnah's personal motivation. R explains Jinnah's choice within the arrangement — a different causal chain from the arrangement's origin.

Value Addition:
• Jinnah died in September 1948, only thirteen months after becoming Pakistan's Governor-General.
• Mountbatten's dual role (plan negotiator and then Governor-General) created a conflict of interest — his influence on Nehru's Kashmir decision (UN referral) is attributed to this proximity.
• Under dominion status, the Governor-General could reserve bills for Crown approval — a real constitutional power, not merely symbolic.

solution.concept_anchor: Chronology of partition events 1946-1947
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because students who know the Direct Action Day and Cabinet Mission are both 1946 events may incorrectly sequence them, or place the Mountbatten Plan announcement before Attlee's declaration.
elimination_logic: Anchor the earliest event: Cabinet Mission Plan was presented in May 1946 — this must come first.
Direct Action Day was August 16, 1946 — after the Cabinet Mission but before Attlee's February 1947 declaration.
Attlee's declaration of February 1947 followed the breakdown of the Cabinet Mission negotiations.
Mountbatten Plan was announced June 3, 1947 — after all three preceding events; Radcliffe Award followed in August 1947.
Correct sequence: Cabinet Mission (1946) → Direct Action Day (August 1946) → Attlee Declaration (February 1947) → Mountbatten Plan (June 3, 1947) → option d.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is in the precise sequencing of the Direct Action Day relative to the Attlee Declaration. Students who remember both as 1946-1947 events sometimes place the Attlee Declaration before Direct Action Day, not realising that Direct Action Day (August 16, 1946) preceded Attlee's announcement (February 20, 1947) — and indeed, the communal violence of Direct Action Day was part of what made Attlee's February announcement urgent.
solution.final_explanation:
The sequence of events leading to partition follows a clear causal chain where each development made the next more inevitable.

Correct sequence: Cabinet Mission Plan → Direct Action Day → Attlee Declaration → Mountbatten Plan (June 3, 1947)

• Cabinet Mission Plan (May 1946): Britain's last attempt to keep India united through a three-tier federal structure. Its failure set the stage for partition.
• Direct Action Day (August 16, 1946): Called by Jinnah to demonstrate Muslim League's resolve. The Great Calcutta Killings followed, triggering a spiral of communal violence that made the British urgency to leave more acute.
• Attlee Declaration (February 20, 1947): Britain announced withdrawal by June 1948 and replaced Wavell with Mountbatten — signalling the end of British mediation and beginning of partition planning.
• Mountbatten Plan (June 3, 1947): The actual partition blueprint, accepted by Congress, Muslim League, and the Sikh representatives, followed by the Indian Independence Act.

Why each wrong option fails:
• Option a reverses the Cabinet Mission and Direct Action Day — Cabinet Mission came first.
• Option b places Attlee Declaration before Direct Action Day — incorrect.
• Option c inverts the Mountbatten Plan and Attlee Declaration positions.

Value Addition:
• The 'Great Calcutta Killings' (August 1946) saw approximately 4,000 deaths in four days — a defining moment in pushing partition forward.
• Wavell's 'Breakdown Plan' (for orderly British withdrawal) was rejected as too pessimistic — leading to his replacement by Mountbatten.
• The interval between the Mountbatten Plan (June 3) and independence (August 15) was only 73 days.

solution.concept_anchor: Lapse of paramountcy accession choice princely states
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students who know Patel integrated most states may assume that accession was automatic or mandatory under the Mountbatten Plan itself, not realising that the plan only declared the lapse of paramountcy — the coercive integration was a subsequent political exercise.
elimination_logic: Identify the constitutional principle: the Mountbatten Plan declared British paramountcy would lapse — states were not automatically merged into either dominion.
Eliminate option a: the plan did not compel automatic accession — integration was a subsequent political and administrative exercise led by Patel, not a provision of the plan itself.
Eliminate option c: the plan did not provide for an independent sovereign status as a third recognised option with ongoing British treaty protections — paramountcy lapsed entirely.
Eliminate option d: the plan did not require a referendum in each state — that was specific only to NWFP and Sylhet.

Confirm option b: upon lapse of paramountcy, each state was legally free to accede to India, Pakistan, or theoretically remain independent — the plan gave them this choice without compelling any specific outcome.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option a exploits students who know Patel ultimately achieved near-total integration and assume this was mandated by the Mountbatten Plan. The distinction between what the plan provided (lapse of paramountcy + free choice) and what Patel accomplished (coercive diplomatic integration) is a classic UPSC trap of conflating the plan's text with its political implementation.
solution.final_explanation:
The Mountbatten Plan's treatment of approximately 565 princely states was deliberately left open-ended, which created the integration problem that Sardar Patel's States Ministry subsequently had to resolve.

Applicable principle: The plan declared that British paramountcy — the legal framework under which Britain had suzerainty over princely states — would lapse on the date of independence. This did not mean states were absorbed into India or Pakistan. It meant the treaty relationships simply ended, leaving states in a legal vacuum.

Mapping to the scenario: A state like the fictional Rampur kingdom would be left free to choose accession to India, accession to Pakistan, or nominal independence — the plan itself imposed no compulsion.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Automatic accession to the geographically contiguous dominion was not a provision of the plan — this was Patel's subsequent political argument, not the plan's legal text.
• Option (b): Correct. The lapse of paramountcy meant states were legally free to accede to either dominion or remain independent, though British advice strongly favoured accession.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Independent sovereign status with continued British treaty protection was not available — paramountcy lapsed entirely, eliminating British treaty obligations.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Referendums were specific to NWFP and Sylhet; no such universal requirement applied to princely states.

Value Addition:
• Patel used the instrument of accession, economic blockade threats, and military force (Hyderabad) to integrate states — tools beyond the plan's provisions.
• Junagadh's ruler acceded to Pakistan despite geographic contiguity with India — demonstrating that 'free choice' was real, if politically untenable.
• The plan's silence on population-transfer for states contributed to the Kashmir crisis when Maharaja Hari Singh delayed his decision.

solution.concept_anchor: Jinnah moth-eaten Pakistan undivided Punjab Bengal demand
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Sind) is a strong distractor because students may think Sind was one of the territories Jinnah was satisfied with receiving intact, not recognising that Sind went to Pakistan without partition — making it the entity Jinnah actually received as demanded.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: territories that Jinnah originally demanded as undivided/whole but received only in partitioned form, prompting his 'moth-eaten Pakistan' characterisation.
Punjab: Jinnah wanted all of Punjab — received only West Punjab (partitioned). Fits the category.
Bengal: Jinnah wanted all of Bengal — received only East Bengal (partitioned). Fits the category.
Sind: Sind went to Pakistan as a complete, unpartitioned province — Jinnah received it whole. Does NOT fit the 'moth-eaten' category.
NWFP: Jinnah received it but only after a contested referendum boycotted by Congress and Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan — the legitimacy was disputed. Fits the disputed/contested category.
Odd one out: Sind — it went to Pakistan intact and was not subject to partition or referendum contestation.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits students who associate 'moth-eaten Pakistan' with all territories that had complications. Sind had a straightforward Legislative Assembly vote in favour of Pakistan with no partition — making it the territory Jinnah received cleanly. Students focused on the 'Muslim-majority province' angle may group Sind with Punjab and Bengal without noting that Sind was not partitioned.
solution.final_explanation:
Jinnah famously described the Pakistan he received as a 'moth-eaten, truncated Pakistan' — referring specifically to the partition of Punjab and Bengal, which denied him the full, undivided versions of these provinces.

• Option (a) — Punjab: Fits the category. Punjab was divided along communal lines, with West Punjab going to Pakistan and East Punjab remaining with India. Jinnah had demanded all of Punjab.
• Option (b) — Sind: Does NOT fit. Sind went to Pakistan as a complete, intact province following a vote by the Sind Legislative Assembly. It was not partitioned. This is the odd one out.
• Option (c) — Bengal: Fits the category. Bengal was divided, with East Bengal forming part of Pakistan and West Bengal remaining with India — another source of Jinnah's 'moth-eaten' complaint.
• Option (d) — NWFP: Fits a related category. Though NWFP joined Pakistan, the referendum was boycotted by Congress and Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, making the legitimacy contested — a different kind of incompleteness.

Value Addition:
• Jinnah's original 'Pakistan Resolution' (Lahore, 1940) envisaged 'independent states' — plural — in the northwest and northeast, not the single partitioned entity he received.
• The partition of Bengal meant that Calcutta, the largest Muslim-population city, remained with India — a significant blow to the League's original vision.
• Sind's clean transfer to Pakistan made Karachi (Sind's capital) the first capital of Pakistan.

solution.concept_anchor: Indian Independence Act 1947 constitutional continuity provision

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Independence Act, 1947 was passed by the British Parliament — not the Indian Constituent Assembly — and it legally constituted both India and Pakistan as separate dominions.
statement_analysis.reason: The Indian Independence Act was enacted by the UK Parliament and received Royal Assent on July 18, 1947. It was a British legislative act that gave legal effect to the Mountbatten Plan by formally creating the two dominions.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Independence Act, 1947 provided that all laws in force in British India immediately before independence would automatically cease to operate after August 15, 1947, requiring the new dominions to legislate afresh.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act explicitly provided for constitutional continuity — existing laws would remain in force until amended or repealed by the new dominion legislatures. This prevented a legal vacuum and ensured administrative continuity, a critical provision given the rushed timeline.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is a strong distractor because students who know about the 'clean break' narrative of independence might assume all British laws were immediately invalidated, making statement 2 seem correct and statement 1 wrong.
elimination_logic: Evaluate statement 1: the Indian Independence Act was indeed passed by the UK Parliament — confirmed. It created two dominions — confirmed. Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate statement 2: the claim that existing laws automatically ceased is factually wrong — the Act specifically provided for continuity of existing laws until replaced. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option c.

Wait — re-checking options: (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) Statement 1 correct Statement 2 incorrect, (d) Statement 1 incorrect Statement 2 correct. Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses the word 'automatically cease' — a scope-extension trap. Students with surface knowledge of independence know that British rule ended on August 15, 1947, and may assume this meant all British-era laws were voided. The critical detail is that the Act built in continuity to prevent administrative collapse — a deliberate provision given the 73-day rushed timeline.
solution.final_explanation:
The Indian Independence Act, 1947 was the British Parliament's legislative instrument translating the Mountbatten Plan into law. Its provisions are frequently tested in UPSC questions because they reveal the careful constitutional engineering behind independence.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Act was passed by the UK Parliament (not India's Constituent Assembly) and received Royal Assent on July 18, 1947. It formally constituted two independent dominions — India and Pakistan — and provided for their governance framework under dominion status.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Act contained an explicit continuity clause ensuring that all laws in force before August 15, 1947 would continue to operate until replaced by the respective dominion legislatures. This was essential to prevent legal chaos — courts, civil services, and contracts all continued under existing frameworks.

Value Addition:
• The Government of India Act, 1935 effectively served as India's interim constitution until the Indian Constitution came into force on January 26, 1950.
• The Indian Independence Act also dissolved the Central Legislature and formally ended the paramountcy over princely states.
• Pakistan's Constituent Assembly took longer to draft a constitution — Pakistan remained under a modified Government of India Act framework until 1956.

solution.concept_anchor: Military assets division 64:36 ratio India Pakistan
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (70:30) is a strong distractor because students who know India received the larger share may estimate a ratio close to 70:30 — a round-number approximation that feels plausible but is incorrect.
elimination_logic: Recall that the military assets division was not equal — India, as the successor state with larger territory and population, received the larger share.
Eliminate option a (50:50): division was explicitly unequal.
Eliminate option c (70:30): this overstates India's share and is not the agreed ratio.
Eliminate option d (80:20): further overstates India's share.
Confirm option b (64:36): the division formula agreed upon was approximately 64% for India and 36% for Pakistan — a ratio derived from proportional assessment of the armed forces.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 64:36 ratio is a precise numerical fact that rewards specific preparation. Students who know India got more but not the exact ratio will gravitate toward the intuitive-sounding 70:30 or default to 50:50 as a 'safe' guess. The trap exploits the tendency to substitute a plausible round number for a precise historical figure.
solution.final_explanation:
The division of military assets between India and Pakistan was one of the most contentious aspects of the partition process, governed by a formula agreed upon by the Armed Forces Reconstitution Committee.

• Option (a) — 50:50: Incorrect. Equal division was not the basis — India, as the larger successor state, received a proportionally larger share.
• Option (b) — 64:36: Correct. The agreed ratio was approximately 64% for India and 36% for Pakistan, reflecting proportional assessment based on the size of the divided forces and territories.
• Option (c) — 70:30: Incorrect. A common approximation error; the actual ratio gave Pakistan a larger share than 30%.
• Option (d) — 80:20: Incorrect. This significantly overstates India's share.

Value Addition:
• Field Marshal Claude Auchinleck was appointed Supreme Commander during the transitional period to oversee the division — his role ended in November 1947.
• Pakistan alleged it did not receive its full 36% share, contributing to early bilateral mistrust.
• The Royal Indian Navy and Royal Indian Air Force divisions were also contested — the RIN mutiny of 1946 had already destabilised naval cohesion before partition.

solution.concept_anchor: Gandhi fast Rs 75 crore payment Pakistan financial dispute
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because Gandhi's fast is well known, but students may associate it with a Hindu-Muslim harmony cause in Calcutta rather than the specific Rs. 75 crore payment dispute — the financial dimension is less frequently recalled.
elimination_logic: Evaluate option a: Gandhi did fast in January 1948, but associating it specifically with halting military operations in Kashmir is incorrect — it was about payment to Pakistan and communal harmony in Delhi.
Evaluate option b: the RBI did serve both dominions initially, but Pakistan established its State Bank in July 1948 — not 'immediately after August 1947.'

Evaluate option c: Gandhi's January 1948 fast is correctly paired with pressure to release the Rs. 75 crore payment to Pakistan that the Indian government had initially withheld — this is the correctly matched pair.
Evaluate option d: Nehru-Liaquat Pact was 1950 (about minority rights), not a financial assets agreement — incorrect pairing.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students know Gandhi fasted in January 1948 but often associate it with communal harmony or the Kashmir situation. The specific connection to the Rs. 75 crore financial dispute (India had withheld the payment amid the Kashmir war) is a precise detail. Option a exploits this by offering a plausible but incorrect cause for the fast.
solution.final_explanation:
The financial partition of British India was among the most contentious post-independence disputes, with the Rs. 75 crore payment becoming politically explosive.

• Option (a): Incorrectly matched. Gandhi's January 1948 fast was not about halting Kashmir military operations — it was about communal violence in Delhi and the release of Pakistan's share of financial assets, including the disputed Rs. 75 crore.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched. The RBI did serve as the monetary authority for both dominions initially, but the State Bank of Pakistan was established in July 1948 — approximately eleven months after independence, not immediately.
• Option (c): Correctly matched. Gandhi undertook his fast in January 1948 in part to pressure the Indian government to release Rs. 75 crore to Pakistan — a payment India had withheld after the Kashmir war began. The government, following Gandhi's fast, agreed to release the funds.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched. The Nehru-Liaquat Pact (1950) addressed minority rights in both countries — it was not a financial assets agreement.

Value Addition:
• Gandhi's January 13, 1948 fast (his last fast) ended after the Indian government agreed to release the funds — he was assassinated 17 days later on January 30, 1948.
• The withholding of Rs. 75 crore was justified by India partly on grounds of the ongoing Kashmir conflict — making it a fusion of military and financial disputes.
• Division of public debt and pension liabilities for British Indian civil servants also formed part of the financial partition negotiations.

Gandhi's Response to the Mountbatten Plan: Opposition and Acquiescence

solution.concept_anchor: Patel truncated India strong centre argument partition acceptance

statement_analysis.statement: Sardar Patel argued that a truncated but strong-centred India was preferable to a loose federation spanning a united but communally divided subcontinent.
statement_analysis.reason: Patel's core argument for accepting partition was pragmatic: a smaller India with undivided Congress authority and a strong central government would be more governable and stable than a united India where Muslim-League-controlled provinces would perpetually contest central authority.

statement_analysis.statement: Gandhi actively campaigned against the Mountbatten Plan by launching a mass civil disobedience movement in the summer of 1947.
statement_analysis.reason: While Gandhi was personally and philosophically opposed to partition ('vivisection of India'), he did not launch any mass movement against it. He trusted Nehru and Patel's political judgment and ultimately did not mobilise public opposition, though he never endorsed the plan.

statement_analysis.statement: C. Rajagopalachari proposed a formula in 1944 that envisaged a partition of India, making him the first prominent Congress leader to publicly suggest dividing the country on communal lines.
statement_analysis.reason: The CR Formula (Rajagopalachari Formula, 1944) proposed that the Muslim League campaign for Pakistan via a plebiscite in Muslim-majority districts and that a sovereign Pakistan be created if the vote favoured it — making Rajagopalachari the earliest Congress figure to publicly engage with the idea of territorial division.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) is a strong distractor because students who know statements 1 and 3 are correct may assume Gandhi's well-known opposition must have taken some organised form, making statement 2 seem plausible.
elimination_logic: Verify statement 1: Patel's 'truncated India with strong centre' argument is a documented historical position — correct.
Verify statement 2: Gandhi opposed partition philosophically but launched NO mass civil disobedience against it — the claim of a 'mass civil disobedience movement' is false.
Verify statement 3: the CR Formula of 1944 is historically documented as the first major Congress engagement with a partition proposal — correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct; statement 2 incorrect → option a (1 and 3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses the phrase 'campaigned against' — a partial-truth trap. Gandhi did oppose partition and spoke against it, but 'launching a mass civil disobedience movement' is factually false. Students who know Gandhi opposed partition emotionally accept the statement without checking whether opposition translated into an organised campaign.
solution.final_explanation:
The Congress Working Committee's acceptance of the Mountbatten Plan was far from unanimous in spirit, even if unanimous in formal vote, reflecting the deep internal tensions within the party.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Patel's pragmatic argument was decisive. He believed that a Congress-governed India without the Muslim League as a permanent coalition partner would be stronger and more efficiently administered than a united India paralysed by communal tensions at the centre.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Gandhi was the most vocal opponent of partition within Congress circles but never translated his opposition into a mass movement. His trust in Nehru and Patel, and his belief that a mass agitation at this stage would cause more bloodshed, led him to acquiesce silently.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Rajagopalachari's 1944 formula was revolutionary in Congress terms — it acknowledged the possibility of Pakistan via a plebiscite and proposed conditions for it. This earned Gandhi's approval at the time but was rejected by the Congress leadership and by Jinnah (who found it insufficient).

Value Addition:
• Gandhi's alternative to partition was to offer Jinnah the Prime Ministership of an undivided India — Nehru and Patel rejected this as politically unrealistic.
• On August 15, 1947, Gandhi fasted in Calcutta rather than celebrating in Delhi — his silent protest against the partition outcome.
• The CR Formula's failure in 1944 demonstrated that even a moderate partition proposal could not satisfy Jinnah, who demanded sovereignty, not a negotiated plebiscite.

solution.concept_anchor: United Bengal proposal Sarat Bose Kiran Shankar Roy rejection
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because Subhas Chandra Bose is far more famous than his brother Sarat Chandra Bose, and students unfamiliar with the United Bengal proposal may default to the Bose name they recognise.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: Maulana Azad opposed partition of India but was not the proposer of a United Bengal plan.
Eliminate option b: Subhas Chandra Bose died in 1945 — he was not present in 1947 to make the United Bengal proposal.
Eliminate option c: Abul Kalam Azad's Frontier proposals are distinct from the United Bengal movement.

Confirm option d: Sarat Chandra Bose (Subhas's elder brother) and Kiran Shankar Roy jointly proposed a sovereign united Bengal that would be neither India nor Pakistan — the proposal was rejected by both Congress and the Muslim League.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap works on the fame differential between Sarat Chandra Bose and Subhas Chandra Bose. Students who recognise 'Bose' in the context of Bengal politics immediately think of Subhas — not his lesser-known but politically active elder brother Sarat Chandra Bose, who was the actual architect of the United Bengal proposal alongside Kiran Shankar Roy.
solution.final_explanation:
The United Bengal proposal of 1947 was an attempt to prevent Bengal's partition by creating an independent, undivided Bengal that would join neither India nor Pakistan.

• Option (a): Incorrect. H.S. Suhrawardy (Bengal's last Muslim Premier) was also involved in United Bengal discussions, but the primary Congress-side proposers were Sarat Chandra Bose and Kiran Shankar Roy.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Subhas Chandra Bose died in a plane crash in August 1945 — he was not alive in 1947 to make any such proposal.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Maulana Azad was a Congress leader who opposed partition of India as a whole, but he did not propose the specific United Bengal formula.
• Option (d): Correct. Sarat Chandra Bose (Subhas's elder brother and a prominent Bengal Congress leader) and Kiran Shankar Roy jointly advocated for a sovereign United Bengal. The proposal was ultimately rejected — by Congress (which feared a Muslim-majority united Bengal joining Pakistan), by the Muslim League (which preferred East Pakistan), and by the Hindu Mahasabha.

Value Addition:
• H.S. Suhrawardy (Muslim League) also supported United Bengal, making it a rare Hindu-Muslim political convergence that nonetheless failed.
• The Hindu Mahasabha actively lobbied for Bengal's partition to prevent Calcutta from falling under Muslim League control.
• The second partition of Bengal (1947) differed from the first (1905): the 1905 partition was reversed in 1911, while the 1947 partition created a permanent international boundary.

solution.concept_anchor: Punjab Boundary Force formation failure Sikh Khalistan demand

statement_analysis.statement: The Punjab Boundary Force was created specifically to prevent communal violence in the districts through which the new international boundary passed, and it succeeded in containing large-scale massacres.
statement_analysis.reason: The Punjab Boundary Force was formed to maintain order in the border districts but failed catastrophically — it was overwhelmed by the scale and ferocity of violence. The massacres that accompanied Punjab's partition were among the worst in human history, directly contradicting any claim of success.

statement_analysis.statement: The Akali Dal and Master Tara Singh initially demanded a separate Sikh state (variously called Khalistan or Sikhistan) during the partition negotiations, but this demand was not incorporated into the Mountbatten Plan.
statement_analysis.reason: Master Tara Singh and the Akali Dal did articulate demands for a separate Sikh homeland during the partition process. The Mountbatten Plan made no provision for such a state, leaving Sikhs divided between India and Pakistan.

statement_analysis.statement: Punjab's partition was less violent than Bengal's partition primarily because Bengal's communal polarisation was far more severe and historically rooted.
statement_analysis.reason: This statement inverts the historical reality. Punjab's partition was significantly more violent than Bengal's — the combination of the Sikh factor, the geography of mixed communities, and the concentration of armed groups made Punjab's violence far more catastrophic. Bengal's partition, while traumatic, saw a slower and more extended displacement rather than the immediate mass massacres of Punjab.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (statement 3 only) is a strong distractor for students who correctly identify statements 1 and 3 as incorrect but stop there, missing that both 1 and 3 are incorrect while 2 is correct — leading them to answer '1 and 3' rather than '1 and 3 only' through option b.
elimination_logic: Evaluate statement 1: the Punjab Boundary Force failed — it did not contain massacres. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate statement 2: the Akali Dal and Master Tara Singh did demand a Sikh state, and the Mountbatten Plan did not provide for it. Statement 2 is correct — exclude from 'NOT correct' answer.
Evaluate statement 3: Punjab was MORE violent than Bengal, not less. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements NOT correct: 1 and 3 → option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a reversed-causation/scope-extension trap — it assigns Punjab's relative violence incorrectly. Students who associate 'Bengal partition of 1905' with historical communal polarisation may assume Bengal's 1947 partition was more violent. Statement 1 exploits students who know the Boundary Force was formed and assume it must have partially succeeded, confusing formation with effectiveness.
solution.final_explanation:
Punjab's partition stands as one of the most catastrophic episodes of communal violence in recorded history, with the Boundary Force's failure a central part of that story.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: The Punjab Boundary Force (approximately 50,000 troops) was designed to protect a 12-mile zone on either side of the new boundary but was swamped by the scale of violence. An estimated 200,000–500,000 people were killed, and 10–12 million were displaced specifically in Punjab — the Boundary Force could not contain it.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Master Tara Singh and the Akali Dal demanded a Sikh homeland (referred to variously as Khalistan or Sikhistan) during the partition negotiations. Mountbatten and the Congress leadership did not accept this demand — Sikhs were left straddling a new international border.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: Punjab's partition was dramatically more violent than Bengal's. The factors include: the Sikh community's unique position (homeland divided), the geography of interspersed communities, the presence of trained former military personnel, and the concentrated nature of mass migrations happening simultaneously in both directions.

Value Addition:
• The Punjab Boundary Force was the only armed force explicitly tasked with communal protection during partition — its failure led to its disbandment in late September 1947.
• Sikh demands for a separate state resurfaced in the 1970s-80s, culminating in Operation Blue Star (1984).
• Approximately 6-8 million Hindus and Sikhs moved from West Punjab to East Punjab, while a similar number of Muslims moved westward — simultaneously, in one of history's largest migrations.

solution.concept_anchor: Constituent Assembly composition changes under Mountbatten Plan

statement_analysis.statement: A new Constituent Assembly for India was constituted after the Mountbatten Plan — the existing assembly (since December 1946) was dissolved and reconstituted.
statement_analysis.reason: The existing Constituent Assembly of India (which had first met in December 1946) was NOT dissolved. It continued as India's Constituent Assembly. Only its membership composition changed — members representing areas going to Pakistan ceased to be members.

statement_analysis.statement: Members elected from constituencies in the areas going to Pakistan ceased to be members of the Indian Constituent Assembly following the Mountbatten Plan.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a direct provision of the plan's implementation. Representatives from areas that would form Pakistan (like East Bengal, Sind, NWFP, West Punjab, Baluchistan) left the Indian Constituent Assembly, and Pakistan's Constituent Assembly was constituted from those representatives.

statement_analysis.statement: Pakistan's Constituent Assembly was newly created under the Mountbatten Plan — it had no pre-existing counterpart unlike India's.
statement_analysis.reason: While India's Constituent Assembly continued from December 1946, Pakistan's assembly was indeed constituted fresh from the partition — members from areas going to Pakistan formed its basis, but unlike India, Pakistan had no pre-existing constituent assembly that simply continued.

statement_analysis.statement: The princely states that acceded to India were immediately given representation in the Constituent Assembly upon the Mountbatten Plan's implementation.
statement_analysis.reason: Representation of princely states in the Constituent Assembly was not immediate or automatic. Negotiations for their representation were separate from the partition process, and many states joined the Assembly gradually as the integration process advanced under Patel.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (only two) is a strong distractor for the correct answer of only two, because students who correctly identify statements 2 and 3 as correct may doubt statement 3 (thinking Pakistan also had some pre-existing body) and incorrectly count only one correct statement.
elimination_logic: Evaluate statement 1: India's Constituent Assembly was NOT dissolved — it continued. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate statement 2: members from Pakistan-going areas did cease to be part of India's assembly. Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate statement 3: Pakistan's assembly was newly constituted — correct.
Evaluate statement 4: immediate automatic representation for princely states was not a provision — incorrect.
Two correct statements (2 and 3) → option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits students who know the partition changed the Constituent Assembly's composition and assume this meant a complete reconstitution. The critical distinction is that India's assembly continued — only its membership contracted. Statement 4 exploits students who know princely states eventually joined the assembly and assume it was immediate.
solution.final_explanation:
The Mountbatten Plan's impact on the Constituent Assembly is a nuanced area — the assembly's continuity was an important constitutional feature.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: India's Constituent Assembly (first convened December 9, 1946) was NOT dissolved or reconstituted. It continued its work — partition simply removed the members from areas going to Pakistan, leaving a smaller but continuous assembly.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Members representing constituencies in West Punjab, East Bengal, Sind, NWFP, Baluchistan, and Sylhet ceased to be members of India's Constituent Assembly. They became the founding membership of Pakistan's Constituent Assembly.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Pakistan did not have a pre-existing constituent assembly — its assembly was constituted fresh from the partition. This contributed to Pakistan's greater constitutional instability compared to India, which had a head start.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Integration of princely state representatives into the Constituent Assembly was gradual and negotiated — it was not immediate or automatic upon the plan's implementation.

Value Addition:
• India's Constitution was adopted on November 26, 1949 and came into force January 26, 1950 — Pakistan did not adopt its first constitution until 1956.
• The Constituent Assembly of India had 299 members at the time of signing the Constitution — considerably fewer than initially planned due to partition-related departures.
• B.R. Ambedkar's appointment as Chairman of the Drafting Committee in August 1947 coincided with the post-partition reconstitution of the assembly's working committees.

solution.concept_anchor: Mountbatten Plan omission population transfer refugee crisis

statement_analysis.statement: The Mountbatten Plan contained explicit provisions for the organised transfer of populations between the two new dominions, recognising that partition would generate large-scale migration.
statement_analysis.reason: The Mountbatten Plan contained no provision whatsoever for population transfer or organised migration. This was a critical omission — the planners hoped communal violence would be contained and did not anticipate 14-15 million people being displaced.

statement_analysis.statement: The scale of displacement following partition — estimated at approximately 14-15 million people — represented the largest forced migration in human history at that time.
statement_analysis.reason: The displacement of 14-15 million people across the Punjab and Bengal borders in 1947-48 is historically recognised as the largest mass migration in human history at that point in time, surpassing all previous recorded population movements.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students who know about the Emergency Committee and Nehru-Liaquat coordination (post-partition bodies) may assume these were planned provisions within the Mountbatten Plan itself, not recognising they were reactive measures created after the crisis emerged.
elimination_logic: Evaluate statement 1: the Mountbatten Plan had no population transfer provisions — the crisis was unplanned. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate statement 2: the 14-15 million displacement figure as the largest in human history at that time is a documented historical claim. Statement 2 is correct.

Wait — re-checking options: (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) Statement 1 incorrect Statement 2 correct, (d) Statement 1 correct Statement 2 incorrect. Statement 1 incorrect + Statement 2 correct → option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses 'explicit provisions' — a scope-extension trap. Students who know that post-partition coordination mechanisms existed (Emergency Committee, Nehru-Liaquat meetings) may infer that some planning existed within the plan itself. The distinction is critical: these mechanisms were reactive emergency measures, not provisions of the Mountbatten Plan.
solution.final_explanation:
The Mountbatten Plan's most consequential failure was not what it included but what it omitted — any mechanism for managing the human displacement that partition would inevitably generate.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Mountbatten Plan made no provision for population transfer or organised migration. This was not an oversight of detail but a fundamental gap — the planners, including Mountbatten, hoped that communal violence would remain contained and that most people would stay in place. The Emergency Committee and Nehru-Liaquat coordination mechanisms were created reactively after the crisis erupted, not as pre-planned components of the partition arrangement.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The displacement of an estimated 14-15 million people between India and Pakistan in 1947-48 was the largest forced migration in recorded human history at that point. The scale dwarfed previous mass movements including post-World War II European refugee flows.

Value Addition:
• The Emergency Committee (established August 1947) was a crisis-response body chaired by Mountbatten as Governor-General — an improvised institution, not a planned one.
• Approximately 200,000-500,000 people were killed during the Punjab migrations alone, with estimates varying significantly.
• Refugee rehabilitation shaped Indian political geography — West Punjab Hindu/Sikh refugees settled heavily in Delhi, Himachal Pradesh, and the canal colonies of East Punjab, permanently altering these regions' demographics.

solution.concept_anchor: British preference two dominions Commonwealth Cold War context
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because the Cold War logic of preferring divided, Commonwealth-bound dominions over a unified neutral India feels causally compelling — students accept R as explaining A without questioning whether this was the stated or primary reason.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Britain preferred the two-dominion outcome within the Commonwealth over a single fully independent India — both dominions initially remained in the Commonwealth.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — R claims that Britain and America feared a Soviet-leaning united India and that partition served Western Cold War interests. This is a contested historical interpretation. While Cold War context existed, the primary British motivation was orderly withdrawal and maintaining Commonwealth ties, not specifically preventing Soviet influence. R as stated overstates the Cold War causation. R is not fully verifiable from the key_dimensions as a primary factual driver — it is an interpretive claim. However, the key_dimensions explicitly state 'British and American concern about a neutral or Soviet-leaning India — how partition served Western interests' — making R factually grounded in the topic's dimensions.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — R offers a Cold War explanation for Britain's preference. But Britain's preference for two Commonwealth dominions was more directly driven by strategic interests in maintaining Commonwealth relationships and naval bases than specifically by preventing Soviet influence. R provides a partial explanation at best — not the primary causal mechanism for A.
A correct + R correct in broad terms + R does NOT fully or primarily explain A → option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both A and R are plausible and largely factual. The trap is the causal link: Britain's preference for two Commonwealth dominions was primarily about maintaining imperial interests, trade relationships, and military access — the Cold War rationale (preventing Soviet influence) was a secondary consideration. Students who know both facts accept the causal link without testing whether it is the primary explanation.
solution.final_explanation:
Britain's strategic calculations in designing the partition outcome reveal a complex interplay of imperial interests, Commonwealth strategy, and Cold War geopolitics.

Assertion (A): Factually correct. Britain strongly preferred that both successor states remain within the Commonwealth — dominion status achieved this. A single fully independent India (as Congress originally demanded — Purna Swaraj) outside the Commonwealth would have ended British strategic and economic interests in the subcontinent.

Reason (R): Factually grounded but overstated as a causal explanation. The Cold War concern about a neutral or Soviet-leaning India was a real consideration in British and American strategic thinking of 1947. However, Britain's primary motivation for preferring two Commonwealth dominions was the continuation of trade relationships, naval base access (e.g., Trincomalee), and strategic influence — not specifically Cold War containment of Soviet influence.

Causal link: R partially explains A but is not the primary or direct explanation. The Cold War rationale was a supplementary justification. The more direct explanation for A was Britain's desire to maintain Commonwealth ties and extract an orderly exit with continuing influence.

Value Addition:
• India left the Commonwealth in 1949 as a republic — but the London Declaration allowed it to remain as a 'republic within the Commonwealth,' setting a precedent.
• Pakistan remained more closely aligned with Western powers (joining SEATO, CENTO) — a geopolitical outcome that arguably served Cold War interests.
• Clement Attlee's Labour government was ideologically committed to Indian independence but was simultaneously managing Britain's post-war economic dependence on American aid — which created pressures toward Cold War alignment.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

Reason (R): British and American strategic planners in 1947 were concerned that a unified independent India might adopt a neutral or Soviet-leaning foreign policy, and the creation of two competing dominions within the Commonwealth better served Cold War Western strategic interests.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct

solution.concept_anchor: Indian Independence Act Royal Assent date July 18 1947
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (August 15, 1947) is a strong distractor because students associate all partition-related dates with August 15 and do not recall that the Indian Independence Act received Royal Assent nearly a month earlier.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a (June 3, 1947): that was the date the Mountbatten Plan was announced — not the Act's Royal Assent date.
Eliminate option c (August 15, 1947): Independence Day was when power was transferred — the Act was already law before that date.
Eliminate option d (July 26, 1947): this date has no special significance in the partition timeline.
Confirm option b (July 18, 1947): the Indian Independence Act received Royal Assent on July 18, 1947 — nearly four weeks before independence was actually transferred.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The most common error is associating all partition legislation with August 15, 1947. Students know August 15 as Independence Day and reverse-engineer that the enabling legislation must also have been finalised on that date. The Royal Assent date (July 18, 1947) is a precise fact that rewards specific preparation and punishes the 'August 15 for everything' assumption.
solution.final_explanation:
The Indian Independence Act moved from announcement to law with remarkable speed — reflecting both political urgency and the efficiency of the British parliamentary process.

• Option (a) — June 3, 1947: Incorrect. June 3 was the date the Mountbatten Plan was publicly announced and accepted by the major parties — not the date of the Act's passage.
• Option (b) — July 18, 1947: Correct. The Indian Independence Act was introduced in the British Parliament in early July 1947 and received Royal Assent on July 18, 1947 — giving it the force of law nearly four weeks before August 15.
• Option (c) — August 15, 1947: Incorrect. August 15 was the date of actual power transfer and independence — the legislative instrument enabling it had already been enacted weeks earlier.
• Option (d) — July 26, 1947: Incorrect. This date has no specific significance in the partition legislative timeline.

Value Addition:
• The Indian Independence Bill was introduced in the House of Commons on July 4, 1947 — American Independence Day — a symbolically noted coincidence.
• The Act was passed with remarkable cross-party support in the UK Parliament, reflecting the post-war political consensus on Indian independence.
• The speed of passage (from June 3 plan to July 18 Royal Assent = 45 days) is itself evidence of the political urgency Mountbatten had created.

solution.concept_anchor: Hyderabad Junagadh Kashmir flashpoints lapse of paramountcy

statement_analysis.statement: The Mountbatten Plan's declaration of the lapse of paramountcy meant that princely states were left in a legal vacuum — they were not automatically merged into either India or Pakistan.
statement_analysis.reason: The lapse of paramountcy dissolved the treaty relationships between the British Crown and the princely states without replacing them with an automatic mechanism of accession. States were left technically free to determine their own futures, creating the integration problem Patel subsequently resolved.

statement_analysis.statement: Hyderabad, Junagadh, and Kashmir became flashpoints precisely because they each had rulers whose religious identity was a minority within their own population, and in each case the ruler's preferred accession choice conflicted with popular sentiment.
statement_analysis.reason: All three states exemplified the religion-population-ruler conflict: Hyderabad had a Muslim Nizam ruling a Hindu-majority state who wanted independence; Junagadh had a Muslim Nawab ruling a Hindu-majority state who acceded to Pakistan; Kashmir had a Hindu Maharaja ruling a Muslim-majority state who delayed accession. In each case, the ruler's position contradicted the demographic majority.

statement_analysis.statement: The Mountbatten Plan explicitly prohibited princely states from declaring independence — they were required to choose between accession to India or Pakistan.
statement_analysis.reason: The Mountbatten Plan imposed no such prohibition. The lapse of paramountcy technically left independence as a legal option, however impractical. It was British advice and subsequent political pressure from Patel (not the plan's text) that discouraged independence claims.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) traps students who know Hyderabad, Junagadh, and Kashmir all became flashpoints and assume statement 3's restriction must logically follow — not checking whether the plan's text actually prohibited independence.
elimination_logic: Verify statement 1: paramountcy lapsing without automatic merger is a well-established fact of partition history. Statement 1 is correct.
Verify statement 2: all three states had the ruler-population religious mismatch described. Statement 2 is correct.
Verify statement 3: the Mountbatten Plan did NOT explicitly prohibit independence — lapse of paramountcy technically permitted it. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct; statement 3 incorrect → option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses 'explicitly prohibited' — a scope-extension technique. Students who know the British strongly discouraged independence for princely states and that Patel's integration drive made independence practically impossible may read this as a formal prohibition within the plan's text. It was not — the plan was silent on prohibiting independence, which is precisely why Hyderabad could attempt it.
solution.final_explanation:
The princely states crisis of 1947-48 was a direct consequence of the Mountbatten Plan's deliberate silence on compulsory integration — a silence that prioritised speed of withdrawal over clarity of outcome.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Paramountcy lapsing created a genuine legal vacuum. The 565 princely states were not absorbed into either dominion by the plan itself — they needed to sign instruments of accession. This vacuum is why Patel's States Ministry and V.P. Menon's work was so consequential.
• Statement 2 — Correct: All three major flashpoints shared the structural feature of a ruler whose religious identity was a minority in his own state. Hyderabad's Nizam sought independence; Junagadh's Nawab acceded to Pakistan; Kashmir's Maharaja Hari Singh delayed accession hoping for independence. Each created a constitutional and military crisis.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The plan did not prohibit independence declarations — it was simply silent on this. Hyderabad's Nizam explicitly claimed independent status for over a year after August 1947, demonstrating that independence was a legally available (if politically untenable) option.

Value Addition:
• Police Action (Operation Polo, September 1948) ended Hyderabad's independence bid — it was the Indian Army's operation, not a provision of the Mountbatten Plan.
• Junagadh's Nawab's accession to Pakistan was reversed by a plebiscite held in February 1948 — showing the 'popular will' principle could be invoked selectively.
• Kashmir's instrument of accession was signed on October 26, 1947 — after Pakistani-backed tribal incursion had already begun.

solution.concept_anchor: Leaders positions on partition 1947 Congress Muslim League
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b swaps the positions of Nehru and Patel on the 'moth-eaten' characterisation, exploiting students who attribute the 'moth-eaten' fear to Patel rather than Nehru.
elimination_logic: Match A (Jinnah): Jinnah called the Pakistan he received 'moth-eaten' because he didn't get undivided Punjab and Bengal — matches description 3.
Match B (Nehru): Nehru expressed the fear that a 'moth-eaten Pakistan' (geographically fragmented) would weaken both nations and create perpetual instability — matches description 1.
Match C (Patel): Patel's argument was specifically about a strong-centred truncated India being preferable to a loose federal India — matches description 4.
Match D (Gandhi): Gandhi's alternative proposal was to offer Jinnah the Prime Ministership of undivided India — matches description 2.
Correct: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap operates between Nehru and Patel. Both accepted partition but for different reasons. Students may attribute Patel's 'strong centre' argument to Nehru or vice versa. The 'moth-eaten' phrase in Jinnah's mouth (List I, A) and as Nehru's fear (List I, B) sounds similar but has different connotations — Jinnah used it as criticism of what he received, while Nehru used it as a concern about Pakistan's viability creating regional instability.
solution.final_explanation:
The acceptance of the Mountbatten Plan by each major figure rested on distinct reasoning — and UPSC questions frequently test whether students can attribute the correct logic to the correct leader.

Correct matches:
• A (Jinnah) — 3: Jinnah famously called the partitioned Pakistan a 'moth-eaten, truncated' state — expressing dissatisfaction that he received only western Punjab and eastern Bengal, not the full, undivided versions.
• B (Nehru) — 1: Nehru's acceptance of partition was reluctant and strategic. He feared that a geographically and economically weak Pakistan ('moth-eaten' in a different sense) would be unstable and create perpetual border crises — ultimately concluding partition with a strong Indian centre was preferable.
• C (Patel) — 4: Patel's argument was the most pragmatic among Congress leaders. He believed a smaller, undivided-Congress-governed India with a strong centre was more governable than a united India permanently contested by Muslim League provinces at the centre.
• D (Gandhi) — 2: Gandhi's alternative was radical — he proposed offering Jinnah the Prime Ministership of an undivided India, believing Jinnah's real goal was power, not territory. Nehru and Patel rejected this proposal as politically unrealistic.

Value Addition:
• Nehru's phrase describing partition as 'a partition of the heart' reflected his deeper pan-Asian federalist vision being sacrificed.
• Patel managed the integration of 565 princely states within one year — vindicating his 'strong centre' argument through practical action.
• Gandhi's Jinnah-as-PM proposal, if accepted, would have produced an India with a Muslim League Prime Minister and a Congress-majority Parliament — a constitutionally novel arrangement.
