solution.concept_anchor: Mountbatten accelerated timeline consequences administrative unpreparedness
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students who know the Radcliffe Award was rushed may conflate 'rushed because of the timeline' with 'Radcliffe was given a legally shorter mandate under the accelerated plan' — not recognising that the reduced timeframe was an administrative consequence, not a legal provision.
elimination_logic: Identify the scenario's core principle: Mountbatten advanced the deadline from June 1948 to August 1947, reducing time from approximately 14-16 months to 2-3 months.

Eliminate option a: the legal mandate given to Radcliffe was not formally shortened — the commission was given the same brief, but the rushed timeline meant it had inadequate time to conduct ground surveys.
Eliminate option c: the military reconstitution was not completed before August 1947 — it was an ongoing process that continued well past independence.

Eliminate option d: the accelerated timeline actually increased (not decreased) communal tensions in the short term — violence erupted precisely because partition happened before administrative frameworks were ready.

Confirm option b: the most significant documented consequence of the accelerated timeline was the Radcliffe Commission having approximately 5 weeks to demarcate boundaries affecting millions of people, with no ability to conduct detailed ground surveys — a direct cause of the boundary disputes and violence.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option a conflates the rushed timeline (a consequence of the accelerated plan) with a formal reduction in Radcliffe's legal mandate. Students who know the Radcliffe Award was hurried may assume this means the commission's legal timeframe was explicitly cut short as a plan provision. In fact, the commission's inadequate time was a consequence of the overall acceleration, not a specifically prescribed shorter mandate.
solution.final_explanation:
Mountbatten's decision to advance the transfer of power from June 1948 to August 1947 — a reduction of approximately ten months — had profound and largely negative consequences for the administrative mechanics of partition.

Applicable principle: Accelerating a complex administrative transition without corresponding institutional preparation creates operational voids that violence and political instability fill.

Mapping to the scenario: Given only 73 days between the plan's announcement (June 3) and independence (August 15), administrative bodies — particularly the Radcliffe Commission — had insufficient time for proper demarcation work.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Radcliffe's legal mandate was not formally shortened as a plan provision — the commission was given the task with the expectation it would complete it. The inadequacy stemmed from operational time pressure, not a legal truncation of mandate.
• Option (b): Correct. The Radcliffe Commission had approximately five weeks of actual working time to demarcate boundaries affecting tens of millions of people across Punjab and Bengal, with no capacity for field surveys. This directly caused imprecise boundary drawing, disputed allocations, and contributed to violence as communities found themselves unexpectedly on the 'wrong' side.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Military reconstitution was explicitly not completed before independence — Field Marshal Auchinleck's Supreme Command continued for months after August 15, 1947.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The accelerated timeline demonstrably increased rather than decreased communal violence in the short term — the mass migrations and massacres of 1947-48 occurred precisely because no administrative buffer existed.

Value Addition:
• Radcliffe had approximately 5 weeks to draw boundaries — he later said he wished he had not taken the task.
• The acceleration was partly motivated by Mountbatten's personal concern about a complete collapse of law and order if partition dragged into 1948.
• The division of the Indian Civil Service between the two dominions was similarly rushed, leaving both governments significantly understaffed.

When Mountbatten advanced the deadline for the transfer of power from June 1948 (as originally specified in the Attlee Declaration) to August 1947, the entire administrative machinery of partition was compressed into approximately 73 days. (b) The Radcliffe Commission had approximately five weeks of actual working time to demarcate boundaries affecting tens of millions of people, making detailed ground surveys impossible and contributing directly to disputed boundary lines

(d) The accelerated timeline reduced communal tensions by giving extremist groups less time to organise resistance, resulting in a calmer immediate transition than a longer drawn-out partition would have produced

solution.concept_anchor: Governor-General constitutional powers dominion status not ceremonial
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students associating 'dominion status' with 'British model' may assume the Governor-General had reserve powers including dissolving Parliament, not recognising that dissolving the Constituent Assembly was not available.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: actual constitutional powers held by the Governor-General under dominion status (Indian Independence Act, 1947).
Option a (reserve bills for Crown approval): this was a real power under dominion status — included in the category.
Option b (assent to or withhold assent from legislation): a standard Governor-General power — included.

Option c (dissolve the Constituent Assembly on advice of the Prime Minister): the Constituent Assembly was a sovereign constituent body, NOT subject to dissolution by the Governor-General — this power did not exist under the arrangement.
Option d (appoint the Prime Minister): the Governor-General did hold this appointment power — included.
Odd one out: option c — dissolving the Constituent Assembly was NOT a Governor-General power.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option c is a plausible-fabrication trap. Students who know the Governor-General could dissolve Parliament in the Westminster model (e.g., dissolving the House of Commons) extend this to the Constituent Assembly, not realising the Constituent Assembly was a sovereign constituent body with a specific mandate — it was not a legislature that could be dissolved at executive discretion.
solution.final_explanation:
The Governor-General's powers under dominion status were real executive powers — not merely ceremonial — but they had specific constitutional limits.

• Option (a) — Reserve bills for Crown approval: A genuine power. Under dominion status, the Governor-General could reserve certain bills for the approval of the British Crown, reflecting the continuing constitutional link. This was a real constraint on full sovereignty.
• Option (b) — Assent to or withhold assent from legislation: A standard Governor-General power drawn from the Westminster model. Withholding assent could effectively veto legislation — a significant executive authority.
• Option (c) — Dissolve the Constituent Assembly: This was NOT a power the Governor-General held. The Constituent Assembly was a sovereign body constituted to draft the constitution — it had its own mandate and was not subject to dissolution by executive action. Conflating the Constituent Assembly with a regular legislature is the trap here.
• Option (d) — Appoint the Prime Minister: The Governor-General did hold appointment powers, including formally appointing the Prime Minister — Mountbatten appointed Nehru in this capacity.

Value Addition:
• Mountbatten's influence on Nehru during the Kashmir crisis (UN referral, October 1947) is the most debated exercise of his Governor-General role — critics argue he exceeded his advisory mandate.
• The Governor-General's real powers made Jinnah's choice of that role (over PM) strategically significant for Pakistan's early governance.
• India became a republic on January 26, 1950, removing the Governor-General role entirely and replacing it with the President.

solution.concept_anchor: Cabinet Mission Plan failure necessitated Mountbatten Plan
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because Jinnah's rejection of the grouping scheme is well known, but students may not know that Congress also effectively torpedoed the plan by rejecting the grouping mechanism while accepting the assembly — making both parties responsible for its failure.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: the Cabinet Mission Plan was not rejected because it proposed dominion status — it actually proposed continuing British oversight, not full independence.

Eliminate option b: while Jinnah's stance was important, the more decisive blow was Congress's acceptance of the Constituent Assembly while rejecting the grouping scheme — this made the plan unworkable.
Eliminate option c: Gandhi's opposition was philosophical but he did not launch an organised movement that caused the plan's failure.

Confirm option d: the Cabinet Mission Plan's fatal contradiction was that Congress accepted the Constituent Assembly but rejected the grouping scheme (which was integral to the plan's federal structure), while Jinnah refused to join an assembly without the grouping guarantees — making the plan unimplementable.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option b conflates Jinnah's role with the plan's collapse. Students who know Jinnah eventually rejected the plan focus on his position and overlook that Congress's selective acceptance (assembly yes, groupings no) was equally — arguably more — fatal to the plan's viability. The plan required both parties' full participation; Congress's rejection of groupings destroyed the federal structure that was the plan's core.
solution.final_explanation:
The Cabinet Mission Plan's failure is among the most consequential political breakdowns in modern Indian history — it made partition structurally inevitable.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The Cabinet Mission Plan did not propose dominion status in the sense of the Mountbatten Plan. It proposed a complex three-tier federal structure — its rejection was not about dominion status.
• Option (b): Incorrect. This is a partial truth. Jinnah initially accepted the Cabinet Mission Plan in June 1946, then withdrew acceptance in July 1946. But attributing the plan's failure solely to Jinnah overlooks the Congress role.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Gandhi expressed reservations but did not organise a movement that caused the plan's collapse.
• Option (d): Correct. The Cabinet Mission Plan's grouping scheme — dividing provinces into three sections (A, B, C) — was inseparable from its federal architecture. Congress accepted the Constituent Assembly but declared it would not be bound by the grouping scheme, interpreting it as advisory. This made Section B (Muslim-majority northwestern provinces) and Section C (Assam and Bengal) unworkable. Jinnah then refused participation without guaranteed groupings. The plan collapsed from irreconcilable selective acceptances.

Value Addition:
• Section B of the grouping scheme included Punjab, NWFP, and Sind — the eventual core of Pakistan.
• Congress's interpretation of the grouping scheme as 'optional' was seen by Jinnah as evidence that Congress would not honour the plan — accelerating his shift toward partition demand.
• Nehru's July 10, 1946 press conference statement that Congress was 'free to change or modify' the constitution was the specific trigger for Jinnah's withdrawal.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
A principal reason why the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 failed — thereby making the Mountbatten Plan and partition unavoidable — was:

(a) The Muslim League rejected the plan because it proposed dominion status rather than full independence for Pakistan, while Congress demanded complete independence for a united India
(b) Jinnah unconditionally rejected the Cabinet Mission Plan from the outset, preventing any serious negotiation of its federal structure
(c) Gandhi organised a mass movement against the Cabinet Mission Plan's grouping scheme, forcing Congress to withdraw its acceptance
(d) Congress accepted the Constituent Assembly but rejected the grouping scheme that was integral to the plan's federal structure, while Jinnah refused to participate without grouping guarantees — making the plan unimplementable

solution.concept_anchor: Sylhet referendum Assam East Bengal demographic impact

statement_analysis.statement: Sylhet was a district of Assam that voted in a referendum to join East Bengal (Pakistan) — the only district-level referendum held during the partition process.
statement_analysis.reason: Sylhet was indeed a district of Assam with a Muslim-majority population. Its referendum resulted in a vote to join East Bengal, which became part of Pakistan. This was the only district-level referendum — all other partition decisions were made at provincial or assembly level.

statement_analysis.statement: The partition of Bengal in 1947 was the first occasion in which Bengal had been divided along administrative lines — the earlier 1905 partition had been a complete reversal that left no permanent boundary.
statement_analysis.reason: The statement is misleading in its implication. While the 1905 partition was indeed reversed in 1911 (leaving no permanent boundary), the 1947 partition was thus the second occasion of Bengal's administrative division — not the first. Calling 1947 the 'first occasion' is factually incorrect.

statement_analysis.statement: Hindu Mahasabha actively supported the partition of Bengal in 1947, contrary to its general stance of opposing partition of India as a whole, because partition prevented Calcutta from being included in a Muslim-majority united Bengal that might have joined Pakistan.
statement_analysis.reason: This is an important historical nuance. The Hindu Mahasabha, while opposing the overall partition of India, supported the partition of Bengal specifically because an undivided Bengal would have been Muslim-majority and might have joined Pakistan — taking Calcutta with it. Their Bengal-specific support for partition was driven by the strategic concern of keeping Calcutta within India.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) traps students who accept the superficially plausible statement 2 without checking whether 1947 was actually the 'first' partition of Bengal.
elimination_logic: Verify statement 1: Sylhet district in Assam, Muslim majority, voted in referendum to join East Bengal — only district-level referendum. Statement 1 is correct.
Verify statement 2: 1905 partition of Bengal is historically documented — 1947 was the SECOND partition, not the first. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify statement 3: Hindu Mahasabha's tactical support for Bengal's partition to save Calcutta is historically documented. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct → option b (1 and 3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a geographic-scope trap exploiting the 'second partition' versus 'first partition' distinction. Students who know Bengal was partitioned in 1947 and know it was later called the 'partition of Bengal' may not recall the 1905 precedent, accepting '1947 as first' without challenge. The 1905 partition's reversal in 1911 is the crucial context.
solution.final_explanation:
Bengal's partition in 1947 must be understood within its own historical trajectory — it was not the first time Bengal was divided.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Sylhet's referendum was unique in the entire partition process — the only time a single district voted on its future independently of the province it was in. Sylhet had a Muslim-majority population despite being part of Hindu-majority Assam, justifying this exception under the Mountbatten Plan's majority-area logic.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 1905 partition of Bengal (by Lord Curzon) divided it into 'Bengal' (Hindu-majority western) and 'Eastern Bengal and Assam' (Muslim-majority eastern). Though reversed in 1911, it was a real administrative partition. The 1947 partition was therefore the second division, not the first.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Hindu Mahasabha's position on Bengal's partition was tactically distinct from its broader anti-partition stance on India as a whole. Leaders like Shyama Prasad Mookerjee argued that a united Bengal joining Pakistan would place Calcutta — then India's largest city and commercial capital — under Muslim League control. Partition of Bengal thus served Hindu Mahasabha's interests in Bengal even while it opposed partition nationally.

Value Addition:
• The 1905 partition was reversed primarily due to the Swadeshi movement — one of the first major mass mobilisations of the nationalist era.
• Calcutta remained with India (West Bengal) — an outcome the Hindu Mahasabha's tactical support for Bengal's partition helped ensure.
• Post-1947 East Bengal (later East Pakistan, then Bangladesh in 1971) went through its own partition journey — making Bengal's division a three-stage historical process.

solution.concept_anchor: Auchinleck Supreme Commander transitional military role
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because Wavell is a familiar name associated with the India transition period, and students may confuse Auchinleck's post-partition Supreme Commander role with Wavell's pre-partition Viceroy role.
elimination_logic: Evaluate option a: Field Marshal Claude Auchinleck was indeed appointed Supreme Commander during the transitional period to oversee division of military assets — correctly matched.
Evaluate option b: Lord Wavell was Viceroy before Mountbatten — he was not involved in the post-partition military asset division.
Evaluate option c: the RBI served as currency authority for both dominions initially, but Pakistan's central bank (State Bank of Pakistan) was established in July 1948, not 'by December 1947.'
Evaluate option d: the military assets division ratio was 64:36 (India:Pakistan), not 60:40.
Option a is correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option b uses Wavell — a real, senior military-political figure closely associated with the India transition — as the entity-swap. Students who know Auchinleck was a Field Marshal in the South Asian context may confuse the two. Wavell's role ended when Mountbatten replaced him as Viceroy in March 1947, whereas Auchinleck's Supreme Command role began at partition and continued into late 1947.
solution.final_explanation:
The transitional military arrangements post-partition required a specific administrative architecture to manage the division of what had been a single unified armed force.

• Option (a): Correctly matched. Field Marshal Sir Claude Auchinleck (famously 'The Auk') was appointed Supreme Commander of all British Indian forces to oversee the reconstitution and division of military assets between the two new dominions. His command technically covered both dominions' forces until they were formally separated.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched. Lord Wavell was Viceroy of India until March 1947, when he was replaced by Mountbatten. He had no role in the post-partition military asset division.
• Option (c): Incorrectly matched. Pakistan established the State Bank of Pakistan in July 1948 — not by December 1947. The RBI continued as the monetary authority for Pakistan for approximately eleven months after independence.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched. The agreed military assets ratio was 64:36 (India receiving 64%, Pakistan receiving 36%) — not 60:40.

Value Addition:
• Auchinleck's Supreme Command was dissolved in November 1947 — his position became untenable when the two dominions went to war over Kashmir.
• The Royal Indian Navy's division was particularly contentious — Pakistan received vessels that were disputed as to their condition.
• Auchinleck was criticised by Indian leaders for allegedly being more sympathetic to Pakistan in the asset division — a charge he denied.

solution.concept_anchor: Gandhi August 15 fast Calcutta opposition acquiescence
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify both A and R as factually true may assume a causal link exists — that Gandhi fasted on August 15 because he opposed partition. While related, R explains Gandhi's psychological state, not the specific choice of Calcutta as his location.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Gandhi spent August 15, 1947 in Calcutta, fasting and praying rather than participating in the Delhi independence celebrations.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Gandhi had been in Calcutta working to calm communal violence and chose to remain there as a moral witness — his fasting on August 15 was indeed connected to his anguish over partition and communal violence.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. Gandhi's presence and fast in Calcutta on August 15 was directly because of the communal situation there and his protest against the vivisection of India — R correctly identifies the causal chain.

A correct + R correct + R explains A → option a. Wait — re-reading A: 'fasting in Calcutta as a silent protest against partition.' R says: 'had been working to calm communal violence in Bengal and chose to remain as a moral witness.' R explains the Calcutta location and the fasting — the causal link holds. → option a.
solution.final_explanation:
Gandhi's decision on August 15, 1947 stands as one of the most powerful individual statements of political dissent through personal conduct rather than organised agitation.

Assertion (A): Factually correct. While Nehru delivered his 'Tryst with Destiny' speech in Delhi and the nation celebrated independence, Gandhi spent August 15 in Calcutta fasting and praying — a deliberate, visible act of dissent from the celebration of a partition he had never accepted.

Reason (R): Factually correct and causally connected. Gandhi had travelled to Calcutta specifically because of the severe communal violence in Bengal. His presence in Calcutta on August 15 was not coincidental — he chose to remain there as a moral witness to the suffering of partition's victims. The fast on that day was a direct expression of his anguish over both the communal violence and the partition itself.

Causal link: R correctly explains A. Gandhi's fasting in Calcutta on Independence Day was causally connected to his work calming communal violence in Bengal and his protest against partition — the two dimensions of R together explain the fact stated in A.

Value Addition:
• Gandhi's presence in Calcutta through the partition period is credited with dramatically reducing violence in Bengal compared to Punjab — his 'one-man army' effect was acknowledged even by Mountbatten.
• On September 1, 1947, Gandhi began another fast in Calcutta when violence reignited — this fast ended when community leaders pledged to restore peace.
• Gandhi's January 1948 fast in Delhi (his last) was about the Rs. 75 crore payment and communal harmony — a different context from the August 1947 Calcutta fast.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequence partition decisions provinces NWFP Bengal Punjab Sylhet
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because students who know NWFP and Sylhet were referendums (and thus 'democratic') may assume they preceded the legislative assembly votes in Bengal and Punjab, not realising the legislative processes and referendums occurred in close succession in the same July 1947 period.
elimination_logic: Anchor: the Mountbatten Plan was announced June 3, 1947 — all province-level decisions followed.
Bengal Legislative Assembly voted in two parts: June 20, 1947 — this was among the first assembly-level votes.
Punjab Legislative Assembly voted in two parts: June 23, 1947 — shortly after Bengal.
NWFP Referendum: July 6-17, 1947 — a separate exercise after the assembly votes.
Sylhet Referendum: June 6-7, 1947 — actually preceded the Bengal and Punjab assembly votes, being held very shortly after the plan's announcement.
Correct chronological order: Sylhet Referendum → Bengal Legislative Assembly → Punjab Legislative Assembly → NWFP Referendum → option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap here exploits the assumption that NWFP referendum preceded the Bengal and Punjab assembly votes because it was a 'bigger' and more contested exercise. In fact, the Sylhet referendum was among the earliest decisions (June 6-7), and the Bengal and Punjab assemblies voted in late June, while NWFP's referendum came in July. Students who sequence by perceived importance rather than actual dates fall into this trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The various partition decisions across provinces were taken in rapid succession in June-July 1947, and their precise sequencing is a testable UPSC detail.

Correct sequence: Sylhet Referendum (June 6-7) → Bengal Legislative Assembly (June 20) → Punjab Legislative Assembly (June 23) → NWFP Referendum (July 6-17)

• Sylhet Referendum (June 6-7, 1947): Held very shortly after the plan's announcement — this district of Assam voted first among all the partition exercises, reflecting its relatively straightforward majority-area logic.
• Bengal Legislative Assembly (June 20, 1947): Members from West Bengal (Hindu-majority districts) and East Bengal (Muslim-majority districts) met separately and voted on their respective futures.
• Punjab Legislative Assembly (June 23, 1947): Same two-part process as Bengal — West Punjab voted to join Pakistan, East Punjab voted to remain with India.
• NWFP Referendum (July 6-17, 1947): Held latest because the NWFP had a Congress ministry under Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, making the referendum politically complex. Congress boycotted; Pakistan won.

Why other options fail:
• Option a reverses NWFP and Sylhet positions.
• Option c places NWFP before Bengal and Punjab assembly votes.
• Option d inverts Bengal and Punjab, and misplaces Sylhet.

Value Addition:
• Sylhet's early referendum date reflects Mountbatten's urgency — even district-level decisions were cleared within days of the plan's announcement.
• The NWFP referendum's July date and Congress boycott made it the most politically charged of all partition decisions.
• Bengal and Punjab assembly votes on consecutive working days (June 20 and 23) reflected the coordinated administrative push.

solution.concept_anchor: Dominion status chosen over full independence governance continuity
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because 'complete sovereignty' sounds like what independence movements demand, and students may assume the Mountbatten Plan granted this — not recognising that dominion status specifically preserved Commonwealth links and was distinct from full republican sovereignty.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a (complete sovereignty outside the Commonwealth): the Mountbatten Plan specifically maintained Commonwealth membership — full external sovereignty was not granted.
Eliminate option b (confederation status): no such intermediate status was proposed — confederation implies shared governance structures not present in the Mountbatten arrangement.
Eliminate option d (protectorate status): a protectorate implies ongoing foreign control, which contradicts the transfer of power.

Confirm option c (dominion status within the British Commonwealth): dominion status was the specific legal form chosen — allowing governance continuity, using the King as head of state, and maintaining Commonwealth membership while transferring executive authority.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option a exploits students who associate independence movements with demands for complete sovereignty. The Mountbatten Plan deliberately chose dominion status over full republican independence because it preserved constitutional continuity (laws remained in force), maintained the existing administrative framework, and kept both new nations within the Commonwealth — a crucial distinction from the 'full independence' Congress had demanded since 1930.
solution.final_explanation:
The choice of dominion status under the Mountbatten Plan was a deliberate constitutional engineering decision with significant practical implications.

• Option (a) — Complete sovereignty outside the Commonwealth: Incorrect. Dominion status was the specific form chosen precisely because it maintained Commonwealth membership and allowed use of existing constitutional frameworks. Full external sovereignty (as a republic outside the Commonwealth) came only later — for India in 1950.
• Option (b) — Confederation status: Incorrect. No confederation arrangement was proposed — this is a plausible-sounding fabrication.
• Option (c) — Dominion status within the British Commonwealth: Correct. Both India and Pakistan were constituted as dominions, with the British monarch as head of state represented by the Governor-General. This allowed existing laws to continue, civil services to function, and an orderly transition without a constitutional vacuum.
• Option (d) — Protectorate status: Incorrect. A protectorate implies ongoing foreign control over certain affairs — the Mountbatten Plan transferred full internal governance to the new dominions.

Value Addition:
• India retained dominion status only until January 26, 1950, when it became a fully sovereign republic — the shortest period any dominion existed before becoming a republic.
• Pakistan remained a dominion until 1956 when its first constitution was adopted.
• The choice of dominion status allowed Mountbatten himself to become Governor-General — a role that would not have existed under full republican independence.

solution.concept_anchor: Congress rejected grouping scheme accepted Constituent Assembly Cabinet Mission

statement_analysis.statement: The Cabinet Mission Plan implicitly accepted the two-nation theory by proposing separate sections (B and C) for Muslim-majority provinces, thereby conceding that Muslim and Hindu interests required separate constitutional treatment.
statement_analysis.reason: The Cabinet Mission Plan explicitly and formally rejected the two-nation theory and rejected Pakistan as a demand. The grouping of provinces into sections was a federal administrative arrangement within a united India — not a concession to the two-nation theory. The Mountbatten Plan was what implicitly accepted the two-nation theory by creating two separate dominions.

statement_analysis.statement: Congress rejected the Cabinet Mission's grouping scheme because it feared that the Muslim-League-dominated sections B and C would effectively function as a state-within-a-state, potentially gravitating toward separation.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the accurate historical explanation for Congress's rejection of the grouping scheme. Sections B (northwestern Muslim-majority provinces) and C (Assam and Bengal) would have been controlled by the Muslim League, giving it effective regional autonomy that Congress feared would be a stepping stone to Pakistan.

statement_analysis.statement: The Mountbatten Plan, unlike the Cabinet Mission Plan, included no mechanism for the princely states to negotiate their relationship with either dominion — paramountcy simply lapsed and states were left without any guidance.
statement_analysis.reason: While it is true that paramountcy lapsed under the Mountbatten Plan, the plan was not completely silent — British advisers (including Mountbatten himself) strongly encouraged states to accede to the geographically contiguous dominion. The plan also set up the framework of instruments of accession. The Cabinet Mission had proposed an advisory negotiating committee, which was indeed a more structured mechanism, but the Mountbatten Plan was not entirely guidance-free.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (2 and 3 only) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify statement 1 as incorrect may also accept statement 3's claim of 'no guidance' at face value, not knowing that Mountbatten did provide strong advisory guidance even if not a formal mechanism.
elimination_logic: Evaluate statement 1: the Cabinet Mission explicitly REJECTED the two-nation theory — calling it 'implicit acceptance' is the opposite of its actual position. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate statement 2: Congress's rejection of the grouping scheme due to fear of League-controlled sections is historically accurate. Statement 2 is correct — exclude from answer.

Evaluate statement 3: the claim that states received 'no guidance' overstates the plan's silence — Mountbatten and British advisers actively guided accession decisions. Statement 3 is NOT fully correct.
Statements NOT correct: 1 and 3 → option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a reversed-interpretation trap: students who know the grouping scheme benefited Muslim-majority provinces may infer the Cabinet Mission 'implicitly accepted' communal division. But the Cabinet Mission formally and explicitly rejected two-nation theory — the grouping scheme was framed as an administrative federal arrangement, not a communal concession. This distinction between formal rejection and practical accommodation is the core trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The Cabinet Mission Plan remains one of history's most complex constitutional proposals — its failure resulted directly from irreconcilable interpretations of its own provisions.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: The Cabinet Mission Plan explicitly and formally rejected the two-nation theory and Pakistan as a demand. Its grouping scheme was framed as an administrative arrangement for a united India — not as acceptance of Muslim separatism. The Mountbatten Plan was the arrangement that implicitly accepted the two-nation principle by creating two dominions.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Congress's opposition to the grouping scheme was precisely this fear — that Sections B and C, under Muslim League dominance, would function as proto-Pakistan regions that could later break away. Nehru's statement that Congress was 'free to modify' the constitution made this fear explicit.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: While the Mountbatten Plan did not create a formal negotiating mechanism for princely states (unlike the Cabinet Mission's advisory committee), it was not without guidance. Mountbatten personally advised rulers to accede to the geographically appropriate dominion, and the instruments of accession framework was the structural mechanism provided.

Value Addition:
• The Cabinet Mission's explicit rejection of Pakistan made it more difficult for Jinnah to reject it outright initially — he initially accepted it in June 1946 before withdrawing.
• Nehru's July 10, 1946 statement effectively killed the Cabinet Mission Plan — it gave Jinnah the justification to withdraw League acceptance.
• V.P. Menon (constitutional adviser) drafted the instruments of accession that formed the practical mechanism for princely state integration — a Mountbatten-era document.

solution.concept_anchor: Mountbatten dual role conflict of interest Kashmir UN referral

statement_analysis.statement: Mountbatten negotiated the partition plan as Viceroy and then served as India's first Governor-General — a role that critics argued created a structural conflict of interest.
statement_analysis.reason: Mountbatten's transition from the negotiating Viceroy to the implementing Governor-General is historically documented as a conflict of interest — he was simultaneously the architect of the plan and the constitutional head of one of the two dominions created by it.

statement_analysis.statement: As India's Governor-General, Mountbatten advised Nehru to take the Kashmir issue to the United Nations — a decision that some historians argue reflected British rather than Indian strategic interests.
statement_analysis.reason: Mountbatten's advice on October 26-27, 1947 to refer Kashmir to the UN is historically documented and contested. Critics, including Sardar Patel, argued this advice served British interests (maintaining balance between the two Commonwealth dominions) rather than India's strategic interests in securing Kashmir outright.

statement_analysis.statement: Jinnah's decision to become Pakistan's Governor-General rather than Prime Minister was primarily motivated by his respect for the Westminster convention that the Prime Minister holds executive power.
statement_analysis.reason: This inverts Jinnah's actual motivation. He chose the Governor-General role precisely because, under dominion status, the Governor-General held real executive authority — not the Prime Minister. Jinnah wanted maximum personal control over Pakistan, and the Governor-General role gave him that power.

statement_analysis.statement: Under dominion status, the Governor-General of India exercised purely ceremonial functions, similar to the constitutional monarch in the fully developed Westminster model.
statement_analysis.reason: Under dominion status as constituted in 1947, the Governor-General held real executive powers — including the power to reserve bills for Crown consideration, withhold assent, and make appointments. The purely ceremonial model developed later; in 1947, these were active constitutional powers.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (only two correct) is the correct answer, but students uncertain about statement 2's UN referral claim may think only statement 1 is clearly correct, selecting option a.
elimination_logic: Evaluate statement 1: Mountbatten's dual role conflict is historically documented. Correct.
Evaluate statement 2: Mountbatten's UN referral advice is historically documented and disputed. Correct.
Evaluate statement 3: Jinnah chose Governor-General FOR executive power, not out of Westminster convention respect — inverted reasoning. Incorrect.
Evaluate statement 4: Governor-General had real powers in 1947, not purely ceremonial. Incorrect.
Two correct statements (1 and 2) → option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 uses 'purely ceremonial' — a scope-extension trap. Students who know the modern constitutional monarchy in the UK is ceremonial may apply this to the 1947 dominion arrangement. But the 1947 Governor-General role was explicitly a real executive position — the ceremonial-only model was not in place. Statement 3 inverts Jinnah's actual logic — a reversed-causation trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Mountbatten's tenure as India's first Governor-General was among the most politically charged constitutional periods in Indian history — his dual role created genuine conflicts that shaped early Indo-Pakistani relations.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Serving as both negotiator (Viceroy) and implementing head of state (Governor-General) is a textbook conflict of interest. Mountbatten's personal relationships with Nehru influenced multiple decisions during this period.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Mountbatten's advice on October 26-27, 1947 to refer Kashmir to the UN — rather than allowing the Indian Army to complete its operations — is one of the most debated decisions of the partition era. Patel and others believed complete military action would have secured Kashmir entirely; the UN referral froze the conflict and created the Line of Control.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Jinnah specifically wanted the Governor-General role because it carried real executive authority under dominion status. His calculation was the opposite of Westminster convention — he chose the role with more power, not less.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: In 1947, under the Indian Independence Act, the Governor-General held active constitutional powers including bill reservation, assent powers, and appointments — not a ceremonial role.

Value Addition:
• India's second Governor-General (and last before becoming a republic) was C. Rajagopalachari (Rajaji) — appointed in June 1948 after Mountbatten's departure.
• The UN referral of Kashmir created the military cease-fire line that became the Line of Control — which has defined the Kashmir dispute to the present day.
• Pakistan's constitution-making was delayed partly because Jinnah's death in September 1948 created a power vacuum at the top of the Governor-General role.

solution.concept_anchor: Population transfer provision absent Mountbatten Plan critical omission
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because the Emergency Committee was a real post-partition coordination body chaired by Mountbatten — students may mistake this reactive crisis body for a 'planned population management commission' within the Mountbatten Plan itself.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: the Mountbatten Plan contained no provision for population transfer — transfer protocol was not part of its design.
Eliminate option c: the Emergency Committee was created reactively after partition, not as a planned provision within the Mountbatten Plan.
Eliminate option d: a 'Minority Rights Commission' of the type described was not established under the Mountbatten Plan.
Confirm option b: the Mountbatten Plan made no provision for population transfer or refugee management — this was the critical omission that contributed to the catastrophic unmanaged migration.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option c names a real institution (Emergency Committee) and a real person (Mountbatten as its chair) but misrepresents it as a planned provision within the Mountbatten Plan. Students who know about the Emergency Committee may accept option c without questioning whether it was pre-planned or reactive. The distinction between designed provisions of the plan and post-crisis improvised institutions is the trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The Mountbatten Plan's most consequential structural gap was its complete silence on population movement — a failure of political imagination that cost hundreds of thousands of lives.

• Option (a): Incorrect. A 'Bilateral Population Transfer Protocol' as a named instrument was not part of the Mountbatten Plan — no such provision existed.
• Option (b): Correct. The Mountbatten Plan made no provision whatsoever for population transfer. The planners — including Mountbatten — assumed that most people would remain in place after partition, with perhaps a manageable minority crossing borders. The actual scale of 14-15 million displaced persons shattered this assumption.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The Emergency Committee (chaired by Mountbatten as Governor-General) was constituted reactively in August-September 1947 to manage the crisis that had already erupted — it was not a planned provision of the Mountbatten Plan announced on June 3, 1947.
• Option (d): Incorrect. A 'Minority Rights Commission' with the powers described was not established under the Mountbatten Plan. Minority rights were addressed in the Indian Constitution and in bilateral agreements like the Nehru-Liaquat Pact (1950) — subsequent to and separate from the Mountbatten Plan.

Value Addition:
• The assumption of no mass migration was shared by almost all political leaders — even Gandhi did not predict the scale of displacement.
• The Nehru-Liaquat Pact (April 1950) was the first formal bilateral mechanism addressing the rights of minorities in both countries — three years after partition.
• Long-term consequences of the unplanned migration included the 'refugee vote bank' that shaped Punjab and Delhi's politics for decades.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Independence Act, 1947 provided for separate Governor-Generals for each dominion but allowed for the possibility of a single shared Governor-General if both dominions agreed to this arrangement.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act did technically allow for a single shared Governor-General if both dominions agreed. Mountbatten had initially proposed serving as a common Governor-General for both India and Pakistan, but Jinnah rejected this — electing to become Pakistan's Governor-General himself. The provision for a common Governor-General was in the Act but was not exercised.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Independence Act, 1947 dissolved the existing Central Legislature of British India and provided that each dominion would be governed by its respective Constituent Assembly until a permanent constitution was adopted.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act did dissolve the Central Legislature and provided that the Constituent Assembly of each dominion would also function as its legislature (a unicameral arrangement) until a permanent constitution was adopted — a dual function that both assemblies exercised.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Independence Act, 1947 specified that the position of Secretary of State for India would continue until 1950, ensuring British oversight of both dominions' governance during the constitutional transition period.
statement_analysis.reason: The Indian Independence Act abolished the office of Secretary of State for India upon the Act coming into force — it did not continue this colonial supervisory role. The abolition of this office was a clear signal of the end of British control over Indian governance.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) traps students who correctly identify statements 1 and 2 as correct and assume the third must also be correct, not knowing the specific fact that the Secretary of State's office was abolished, not continued.
elimination_logic: Verify statement 1: the provision for a common Governor-General (if agreed by both) was in the Act — Jinnah's rejection meant it wasn't used, but the provision existed. Statement 1 is correct.
Verify statement 2: the Central Legislature was dissolved and Constituent Assemblies became the legislative bodies — correct.
Verify statement 3: the Secretary of State for India was abolished by the Act, not continued until 1950. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct → option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a plausible-sounding continuation date (1950, when India became a republic) to suggest the Secretary of State's office persisted. Students who know the Secretary of State was a colonial-era supervisory role may assume some transition period continued it. The Act's immediate abolition of this office is a specific fact that rewards precise preparation.
solution.final_explanation:
The Indian Independence Act, 1947 is the foundational legislative document of Indian independence, and its specific provisions are frequently tested in UPSC questions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Act included a provision allowing for a single common Governor-General for both dominions if both agreed. Mountbatten proposed this arrangement — he was willing to serve both dominions simultaneously. Jinnah's rejection forced the separate appointments, but the legal provision for a common Governor-General was in the Act.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Act dissolved the Central Legislature of British India. In its place, each Constituent Assembly was given the power to legislate for its dominion — functioning simultaneously as a constitutional drafting body and an ordinary legislature until a permanent constitution was adopted.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Indian Independence Act explicitly abolished the office of the Secretary of State for India — a colonial-era position that exercised supervisory control over the Viceroy and Indian governance. Its abolition was a constitutional recognition of the end of British oversight. The year 1950 has no relevance to the Secretary of State's office in this context.

Value Addition:
• The Secretary of State for India had been a Cabinet-level position since 1858 (following the Government of India Act, 1858 transferring power from the East India Company to the Crown).
• The Constituent Assemblies' dual role as legislatures and drafting bodies created some constitutional friction — urgent legislation had to be prioritised alongside the constitutional drafting work.
• India's Constituent Assembly completed its drafting work and adopted the Constitution on November 26, 1949 — it came into force January 26, 1950.

statement_analysis.statement: Clement Attlee's Labour government was the first British government to formally commit to granting India full independence — previous Conservative governments had only offered varying degrees of self-governance within the British Empire.
statement_analysis.reason: The Attlee-led Labour government's February 1947 declaration and the subsequent Indian Independence Act, 1947 represented the first formal British commitment to full transfer of power. While earlier arrangements (Montagu-Chelmsford, Government of India Act 1935) had expanded self-governance, none constituted a formal commitment to complete independence — that came under Attlee.

statement_analysis.statement: Britain's preference for both India and Pakistan to remain within the Commonwealth was purely driven by ideological commitment to maintaining cultural ties with former colonies — strategic and economic factors played no significant role in this preference.
statement_analysis.reason: Britain's Commonwealth preference was significantly driven by strategic and economic factors: maintaining trade relationships, retaining access to military bases (e.g., Trincomalee), preserving sterling area economic ties, and continuing strategic influence in the Indian Ocean region. The claim that 'strategic and economic factors played no significant role' is factually incorrect — they were among the primary drivers.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students who accept statement 1 as obviously correct (Labour = independence) may also accept statement 2's 'ideological' framing without checking whether strategic factors are dismissed — the scope-extension in 'no significant role' is easily missed.
elimination_logic: Evaluate statement 1: Attlee's Labour government did make the first formal commitment to complete independence — previous reforms fell short of this. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate statement 2: 'purely ideological' and 'no significant role' for strategic factors are scope-extension qualifiers that make this false — strategic interests were central to Commonwealth membership preference. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option c.
Re-checking options: (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) Statement 1 correct Statement 2 incorrect, (d) Statement 1 incorrect Statement 2 correct → option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's scope-extension trap uses the phrase 'purely ideological' and 'no significant role' — classic UPSC all-or-nothing qualifiers that convert a partially true statement into a false one. Students who know Attlee was ideologically committed to independence accept the ideological framing of statement 2 without noticing that the second clause dismisses strategic factors entirely — which is historically inaccurate.
solution.final_explanation:
Britain's handling of Indian independence under Attlee reflects a complex intersection of ideology, strategic interest, and economic calculation that defies simple characterisation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Labour government under Attlee did represent a qualitative shift in British commitment. The Government of India Act 1935, the Cripps Mission (1942), and the Cabinet Mission (1946) were steps toward self-governance but not full independence. The February 1947 declaration and Indian Independence Act constituted the first formal, unconditional commitment to complete transfer of power.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Britain's preference for Commonwealth membership was not 'purely ideological.' Strategic factors were central: Trincomalee naval base (Ceylon), Indian Ocean strategic positioning, sterling area trade relationships (India held significant sterling balances), and the desire to maintain influence in a Cold War world without the formal costs of empire. The ideological commitment to independence coexisted with — and was often subordinated to — these strategic calculations.

Value Addition:
• India's sterling balances (accumulated during WWII) gave Britain economic leverage — India held approximately £1.3 billion in sterling balances in 1947, a significant claim on British reserves.
• Britain retained Trincomalee naval base (Ceylon) and Karachi as strategic facilities even after partition — demonstrating the strategic dimension of the Commonwealth arrangement.
• Attlee's government simultaneously managed Indian independence and the post-war economic recovery under Marshall Plan assistance — creating the dual pressure of strategic and economic considerations.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap pairs the 1905 Bengal partition detail (description 3) with Sarat Bose (List I, D) in wrong options, exploiting students who associate all Bengal-related content together. Students who know Sarat Bose proposed United Bengal may incorrectly match him with the 1905 partition description, not realising his proposal was a 1947 alternative to partition — entirely separate from the 1905 event.
solution.final_explanation:
The partitions of Bengal and Punjab — and the resistance to partition they generated — are distinct historical episodes with different characters, actors, and consequences.

Correct matches:
• A (First partition of Bengal, 1905) — 3: Lord Curzon's 1905 partition divided Bengal into a Hindu-majority western Bengal and 'Eastern Bengal and Assam' with a Muslim majority. This partition was reversed in 1911 following the Swadeshi movement — India's first major mass mobilisation.
• B (Sikh factor in Punjab's partition, 1947) — 1: The Akali Dal under Master Tara Singh demanded a separate Sikh state (Khalistan or Sikhistan) during the 1947 negotiations. This demand was not accommodated in the Mountbatten Plan — Sikhs were divided between India and Pakistan, with the community's homeland split along the new boundary.
• C (Punjab Boundary Force) — 4: The Punjab Boundary Force was established specifically to maintain order in the districts adjacent to the new international border. It was eventually overwhelmed by the scale of violence — approximately 50,000 troops proved inadequate for protecting millions of migrants.
• D (Sarat Chandra Bose's United Bengal proposal, 1947) — 2: Sarat Bose and Kiran Shankar Roy proposed a sovereign United Bengal independent of both India and Pakistan. This proposal was rejected by Congress (feared Muslim-majority united Bengal joining Pakistan), the Muslim League (preferred East Pakistan), and the Hindu Mahasabha.

Value Addition:
• The 1905 partition's reversal in 1911 is seen as the first major nationalist victory against British divide-and-rule policy.
• Master Tara Singh later became a prominent figure in the Punjabi Suba movement (1960s), which eventually achieved a Punjabi-speaking state.
• The Punjab Boundary Force was disbanded in late September 1947 after proving insufficient — responsibility for security reverted to the two dominions' separate armies.
